Under the Clean Water Act, 2006, areas where drinking water sources are vulnerable to human activities occurring on the land surface have been mapped. Planning policy protects the water resources in these areas from degradation.

Impervious surfaces are mainly artificial structures such as pavements, roads, sidewalks, driveways and parking lots that are covered by impenetrable materials such as asphalt, concrete, brick, and stone. Soils compacted by urban development are also highly impervious. 

The Impervious Surface Area layer provides the percent impervious for each square km, that were used to assess drinking water threats, related to the application of road salt.
